title: Easy exam 1
about: Ten single-choice questions on the basics: one concept each, with the classic look-alike options.

questions.title: Boot sequence
questions.text: Which statement about the boot sequence of a PC is FALSE?

options.t: The kernel starts first and is the one that initialises the firmware and loads the boot loader.
options.why: It is the other way round: the firmware (UEFI/BIOS) runs first, then the boot loader, and the boot loader loads the kernel.

options.t: The firmware initialises the hardware and finds the boot device before any boot loader code runs.
options.why: True: the firmware is the first code to execute after power-on.

options.t: The boot loader loads the kernel into memory and then hands control over to it.
options.why: True: that is the boot loader's job (GRUB on most Linux systems).

options.t: The first process started by the kernel gets PID 1 and is in charge of bringing up the services.
options.why: True: today that process is usually systemd.

questions.title: Background job
questions.text: You type `sort bigfile > sorted &`. What happens?

options.t: The prompt returns at once and `sort` keeps running in the background, writing into `sorted`.
options.why: `&` only decides whether the shell waits; the `>` redirection still applies.

options.t: The prompt returns only when `sort` ends, because `&` just controls where the output goes.
options.why: `&` has nothing to do with the output: it tells the shell not to wait for the command.

options.t: `sort` starts suspended and does nothing until `fg` or `bg` is typed.
options.why: A job started with `&` runs immediately; suspended jobs are the ones stopped with `Ctrl+Z`.

options.t: `&` sends the result of `sort` to the screen instead of to `sorted`.
options.why: Output goes where `>` says: the file `sorted`.

questions.title: Counting lines
questions.text: `names.txt` has 3 lines. Which command prints only the number `3`, without the file name?

options.why: With the input redirected, `wc` does not know the file name, so it prints just the count.
It prints the count followed by the file name: `3 names.txt`.
`-w` counts words, and the file name is still printed.
`-c` counts bytes, and the file name is still printed.

questions.title: Relative paths
questions.text: Your current directory is `/home/ana/docs`. Which statement is TRUE?

options.why: `..` is the parent directory, so `../notes` is `/home/ana/notes`.
`.` is the current directory: `./notes` is `/home/ana/docs/notes`.
`~` is the home directory, so `~/notes` is `/home/ana/notes` for ana, not a path under `docs`.
A path starting with `/` is absolute and starts at the root: `/notes`.
Single quotes block the expansion of `$name`; double quotes allow it.
Single quotes keep `$name` as literal text.
Double quotes still expand variables.
The quotes are swapped in this option: single quotes are the ones that stop the expansion.

questions.title: Running a script without execute permission
questions.text: `hello.sh` is in the current directory with permissions `rw-r--r--`, and `.` is not in the `PATH`. Which command runs it without changing its permissions?

options.why: `bash` reads the file as data, so the file only needs to be readable.
The shell tries to execute the file itself: "Permission denied", since it has no `x`.
Without a path the shell only looks in the `PATH`, which does not include the current directory: "command not found".
That file does not exist in `/bin`: "No such file or directory".

options.t: It is the administrator account, identified by UID 0.
options.why: The kernel looks at the UID, which is 0 for root.

options.t: It is the first account created at installation and has no special privileges.
options.why: It is the administrator and it does have special privileges.

options.t: Any user that belongs to the group `root` is a superuser.
options.why: Privileges follow the UID 0, not the membership of a group named `root`.
It is `/root`, outside `/home`.

questions.title: Hidden files
questions.text: Which command lists the current directory in long format including the hidden files?

options.why: `-a` shows the entries whose names start with a dot and `-l` gives the long format.
Long format, but hidden files are not shown without `-a`.
`-R` is recursive, not "all"; hidden files stay hidden.
`-d` lists the directory entry itself instead of its contents.

questions.title: Reading a mode string
questions.text: `ls -l` shows `-rwxr-x--- 1 ana dev 120 Mar 3 10:00 run.sh`. Which statement is FALSE?

options.t: Users who are neither ana nor members of `dev` can read the file.
options.why: False: the last three characters (others) are `---`, so they cannot read, write or execute it.

options.t: ana can read, write and execute it.
options.why: True: the owner has `rwx`.

options.t: Members of `dev` can read and execute it but not modify it.
options.why: True: the group has `r-x`.
True: the first character is `-` (a directory would show `d`).

questions.title: Several commands on a line
questions.text: What does `echo A; echo; echo B` print?

options.t: Three lines: `A`, an empty line and `B`
options.why: `;` separates commands and `echo` with no arguments prints just a newline.
The second `echo` is not skipped: it prints an empty line.
Each `echo` ends its output with a newline.

options.t: An error, because of the empty `echo`
options.why: `echo` without arguments is valid.
